sources.title: Donald Burry, A History of the Taylor Statten Camps (MA thesis, U of Saskatchewan, 1985)
sources.notes: Read in full (178pp, downloaded PDF + pdftotext), 2026-07-09. Advisor John Dewar, committee Howard Nixon/Val Schneider. New Taylor Statten biographical detail: full birth name 'Emerson Taylor Israel Statten,' born July 12 1882 in his grandfather's Springfield/Erindale ON exchange hotel; parents John Marr Statten and Eleanor Elmina (nee Taylor) Statten; siblings Bolina 'Bay' (b.1884), Waldemar 'Waldie' (b.1887), Lincoln (b.1889); joined YMCA 1902 via J. Howard Crocker's Leaders' Corps; Secretary of Boys' Work, Toronto Central YMCA, May 1 1905-1911; ran 'Camp Tuxis' (closed Aug 1920) immediately before founding Ahmek (1921); died in his sleep Nov 1 1956 at Little Wapomeo after a day gardening (per a Statten-family Christmas letter quoted in the thesis). Identifies the underlying full biography: C.A.M. Edwards, 'Taylor Statten: A Biography' (Ryerson Press, 1960, 161pp) -- not digitized anywhere (checked HathiTrust, Internet Archive). Zero mentions of 'Kanawana' or 'Naismith' anywhere in the full text -- does not address whether Statten ever visited Kanawana. Contains an internal three-way conflict on the Ontario Camping Association's founding date -- see kb/conflicts.json c_019.

Distinguish from RPCQ id 93576 ('Site du patrimoine de Saint-Sauveur-des-Monts'), confirmed by a separate 2026-07-09 sweep to NOT mention Kanawana, and from id 235860 ('Chapelle du Camp Canawish'), an unrelated 1898 chapel in Rivière-Ouelle -- a name-similarity false lead, not to be re-investigated.

Possible future stub candidate ('recurring event or tradition') once 5+ facts accumulate -- see priorities.json.

sources.notes: Expired job listing for an inclusion-support staff role: supervises one assigned camper with special needs all day (meals, activities, personal care), sleeps in the camper's cabin/tent, plans activities across the four 12-day sessions. Requires French + intermediate English, First Aid/CPR, clean criminal record.

sources.title: "Director, Outdoor Education Centre Kanawana" job listing (Glassdoor)
sources.notes: Direct page fetch returned 403; title/existence confirmed via search-result snippet only, not the full listing text. Flagged for independent re-verification -- do not treat as fully corroborated until a direct fetch or a second independent source confirms it (see priorities.json).

sources.title: "Where Will Your History MA Take You?" — Concordia History Department event page, March 25, 2024
sources.notes: Panelist listing for a Concordia History MA careers event names Grace McMorris (author of the 2023 Kamp Kanawana thesis) as a 'recent graduate' with affiliation 'Historica Canada.' No further career detail given.

sources.title: Camp Kanawana reviews — CampRatingz.com
sources.notes: 9 anonymous user-submitted reviews, average 3.8/5, spanning 2007-2014. Mostly positive testimonials. One 2012 review, self-described as from a 'former 9-year staff member,' alleges expired medications and mishandled medical emergencies; a 2010 review alleges an unaddressed injury. These are unverified, anonymous, user-generated allegations -- NOT integrated into kb/facts.json as substantive claims per operator-review policy for sensitive/unverified content. See priorities.json (p_194) for the flagged human-review item. Only the platform's existence and aggregate rating are treated as stated fact (f_1823).

sources.title: Serment du campeur / Camper's Oath (Camp YMCA Kanawana, 2010 and 2013 bilingual versions)
sources.notes: Recovered via a ymcaquebec.org PDF crawl that also scanned Wayback CDX for the camp's predecessor domains (ymcakanawana.com/.ca). Full bilingual text of the formal Camper's Oath, nearly identical across the 2010 and 2013 captures. Tied explicitly to the camp motto 'Non Nobis Solum.' Signed by every participant and parent/guardian; kept on file at the camp office.

sources.title: "Reportage vécu" — Rob Braide camper testimonial (Camp YMCA Kanawana recruitment document, 2007)
sources.notes: Bilingual testimonial by Rob Braide, President of Standard Broadcasting Corporation (CHOM, MIX 96, CJAD), camper for 9 summers, describing a 1967 age-14 canoe trip retracing the Deep River-Ottawa fur-trade route (150 miles, week-long, 6 other boys plus a counsellor). Published as camp recruitment material.

sources.title: 2005 Parent Handbook, Camp YMCA Kanawana (English, .doc)
sources.notes: Recovered via Wayback CDX scan of the predecessor ymcakanawana.com domain. Full 2005 parent handbook: 1435 Drummond St. Montreal / 673 montée Saint-Elmire St-Sauveur addresses, fee/refund policy, canoe-trip safety protocol (satellite phone, radio, route plans filed with park authorities). Document author metadata reads 'aboyer' -- a plausible but unconfirmed reference to Arleen Boyer (Executive Director 1995-2000, see directors-index.md); the document postdates her documented tenure by ~5 years, so this is a lead, not a confirmation (she may have continued authoring administrative templates as a volunteer, or the metadata may be inherited from an older template).

sources.title: Staff application form, Camp YMCA Kanawana (2006)
sources.notes: Recovered via Wayback CDX scan of the predecessor ymcakanawana.com domain. Lists 'sean.day@ymcamontreal.qc.ca' as the staff-application contact -- confirms Sean Day held some staff/administrative role at Kanawana by 2006, though a contact-email listing does not by itself establish the Director title. Relevant context (not resolution) for conflict c_017 (Sean Day's documented directorship start, 2005 vs. 2008).

sources.title: Camp Kanawana Preparation Guide, Summer 2026 (parent handbook, EN/FR, current authoritative version)
sources.notes: Found live on ymcaquebec.org (created 2026-06-16), superseding both the January 2026 and 2025 preparation guides already cached (src_kk_prep_guide_2025). Same 43-page structure per a site-crawl agent's comparison; the canoe-trip complement is embedded in this same PDF (pages 29+), not a separate document. Not yet re-extracted in full -- flagged as future work (the 2025 version's site-map legend and staff-team facts are still current per this campaign's spot-checks, but a full re-diff has not been done). | 2026-08-25 (p_273): the priority recorded this as already cached; it was NOT -- cache_path was null and no file existed on disk. Downloaded (8.77 MB PDF), extracted (74,071 chars) and cached, along with the FR edition and the 2025 guide for diffing.

sources.title: ymcakanawana.com / ymcakanawana.ca predecessor-domain document cache, 2005-2015 (Wayback CDX catalogue)
sources.notes: A Wayback CDX prefix scan of the camp's predecessor domains surfaced ~20 additional documents not yet deep-extracted: French/English parent guides for 2009 (already cached), 2010, 2011, 2012, 2014 (regular + expedition), an undated LIT guide, packing lists (2005, 2013), maps to camp (2005, 2012, 2014), payment/donation/registration forms (2005), and a 2015 sessions-and-rates sheet confirming the 'Fonds Sam Lazarus' name for unspent tuck-account donations. Downloaded copies retained in the session scratchpad. Flagged as a future extraction pass (see priorities.json) rather than fully mined this campaign, since their content substantially overlaps already-documented program/fee/policy facts from later years.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1890-91 (presented May 28, 1891)
sources.notes: Part of a 165-item digitized Montreal YMCA Annual Report collection on Internet Archive (identifiers 'sgw-ymca-annual-report-YYYY'), not previously catalogued in this KB. States the Association secured 'Mr. W. H. Ball as Physical Director,' a Springfield School graduate, commencing September 1891; separately identifies him as 'Mr. W.H. Ball, jr., of Yonkers, N.Y.' Key primary source for the Billy Ball identity question (see f_1829).

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1902
sources.notes: Same digitized Annual Report collection as src_ia_ymca_annual_1890_91. States: 'Mr. W. H. Ball, the Association's first Physical Director, who rendered such helpful service during the past ten years... resigned and accepted a similar position with the Prospect Park Branch of the Brooklyn Association. He was succeeded by Mr. J. E. Merritt.' Confirms a ~10-year Montreal tenure (1891-1901/1902).

sources.title: Lovell's Montreal Directory, 1893-94
sources.notes: Independent (non-YMCA-produced) corroboration of W.H. Ball as YMCA of Montreal physical director: institutional listing 'YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION, D.A. Budge, general secretary; T.D. Patton, asst secretary; W. H. Ball, physical director, Dorchester cor Dominion Sq,' plus a separate residential street-directory line 'Ball W. H., physical director Y.M.C.A.'

sources.title: Camp Otoreke Blog (self-published alumni blog, est. 2005)
sources.notes: Self-published blog by former Camp Otoreke staff, with anonymous/pseudonymous commenters ('Michael Evans,' 'Finn Sander,' 'Howard Duncan'). No independent corroboration found for any claim on this blog. Used cautiously: existence and general post-closure narrative treated as stated fact with an explicit low-reliability flag; the specific staff-name roster (Huppfield/McGerrigle/Mackay) should NOT be used to spawn biography stubs without independent verification (YMCA annual reports, obituaries) per CLAUDE.md's formal-RALPH requirement for people stubs.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1930 (covering the 1929 season)
sources.notes: Part of the same 165-item digitized Annual Report collection as the Billy Ball sources above. Documents the 1929 build-out of Lac Becscies as a Kanawana annex/overflow site (wharf, dining pavilion, four tent floors, well) explicitly 'for peak periods and also for overnight and short term out-trips'; also documents 1929 capital spending ($2,258 on 'the Becscies extension and the new craft shop,' combined figure) and Westmount Branch businessmen underwriting twelve Protestant Orphans' Home boys as regular campers that season.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1934 (covering the 1933 season)
sources.notes: States the Protestant Orphans' Home 'was given the free use of our auxiliary camp equipment at Lac Becscies' for the 1933 season, names W.H. Spearman as that season's Kanawana Camp Director.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1935 (covering the 1934 season)
sources.notes: Repeats the Protestant Orphans' Home free-use-of-Lac-Becscies arrangement for the 1934 season, same wording as the 1934 report.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1936 (covering the 1935 season)
sources.notes: Repeats the Protestant Orphans' Home free-use-of-Lac-Becscies arrangement for the 1935 season.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1937 (covering the 1936 season)
sources.notes: Final documented year of the Protestant Orphans' Home / Lac Becscies arrangement: 'again given, free of charge, the use of our property on Lake Bec-scies, for which their Board has expressed generous appreciation.' Names W.J.G. Macdiarmid as that season's Kanawana Camp Director -- independently corroborating the already-documented director (see directors-index.md, Greig/W.J.G. Macdiarmid, 1935-1938+). Also documents Kanawana's own record 1937-38 attendance (407 boys, 1,442 camper-weeks).

sources.title: "Camp Amy Molson: a history of the Summer Camp of the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society" (McGill eScholarship)
sources.notes: Accessed only via search-engine summary, not full text. Documents Camp Amy Molson's founding May 23, 1944 by the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent Society as a dedicated summer camp for children from foster homes/orphanages (58 campers, 5 counsellors, first season). A plausible but unconfirmed contributing thread to the Camp Becsies 1936-1960 gap -- does not cleanly explain it (7-8 year unexplained span remains, and the Ladies' Benevolent Society and Protestant Orphans' Home were still separate organizations at the relevant date).

sources.title: Batshaw Centre History (batshawcentreshistory.ca) -- Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home / Ladies' Benevolent Society institutional history pages
sources.notes: Retrieved only via search-result summaries; direct WebFetch of the source pages returned HTTP 503 twice. States the Montreal Protestant Orphans' Home was founded 1822 as the Protestant Orphan Asylum, built a permanent home in 1849, moved to Summerhill/Cote-des-Neiges in 1894, and merged with the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent Society around 1946 or 1947 (sources disagree on the exact year) to form the Montreal Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society, later Summerhill Homes. Needs independent verification against the live page before being treated as fully confident, especially the exact merger year.

sources.title: Wikipedia, "Woodcraft League of America"
sources.notes: General/national context on the organization Kanawana chartered a tribe in circa 1922 -- peak membership ~5,000 (1920s-30s), decline during WWII-era militarism/industrialization, dissolution in 1946 after founder Ernest Thompson Seton's death. Not Kanawana-specific; cross-referenced against the Ernest Thompson Seton Institute (etsetoninstitute.org) and Inquiry Net (inquiry.net).

sources.title: Trent University Archives finding aid — Mary S. Edgar fonds (82-010)
sources.notes: Full biographical finding-aid description: parents Joseph Edgar/Mary Little; education Sundridge Public School -> Barrie High School -> Havergal Ladies College -> Univ. of Chicago extension -> Teachers College Columbia -> YWCA National Training School NYC (1915); YWCA 'First National Girls' Work' role 1912-1914; 4-month YWCA Japan posting 1920; purchased Lake Bernard property 1920 (2 years before Glen Bernard Camp opened 1922); 4 books (Wood-fire and Candlelight 1945, Under Open Skies 1956, The Christmas Wreath of Verse 1967, Once There Was a Camper 1970); fonds donated by nephew John Gilchrist, originals at Queen's University Archives, Trent holds photocopies 1920-1970.

sources.title: Library and Archives Canada — Montreal Young Women's Christian Association fonds
sources.notes: Catalog description only, NOT yet accessed/extracted -- a strong new lead. Contains a dedicated series 'Camp Oolahwan committee minutes, reports and training programmes, 1916-1974,' plus Committee minutes (1910-1973), Finance (1918-1975), Reports (1877-1972), and photographs (1937-1973). Confirms Montreal YWCA founding date May 24, 1874. Flagged in priorities.json as a future source-ingestion target -- could resolve Camp Oolahwan's capacity, age range, and post-Halliday directors.

sources.title: McCord Stewart Museum — Junior League of Montreal fonds (P685)
sources.notes: Fonds description (accessed via search snippet; direct page fetch returned 403/503): Junior League of Montreal founded 1912; its camp founded 1921, financed partly via a 1930-31 campaign that also funded a Griffintown dental clinic and hospital canteens; welcomed 300+ girls/year by the early 1960s, ~12,000 girls total. States 'today, Camp Amy Molson carries on its mission' -- a continuity claim in tension with Camp Amy Molson's own official history (founded 1944 by the Ladies' Benevolent and Protestant Orphans' Society, not the Junior League). See conflict c_018 in kb/conflicts.json.

sources.title: Elise Chenier, "Class, Gender, and the Social Standard: The Montreal Junior League, 1912-1939," Canadian Historical Review 90.4 (2009)
sources.notes: Academic article (pp. 694, 702 cited) documenting the Junior League of Montreal's history, including its 1921 summer camp for underprivileged girls. Accessed via search-result citation detail, not full text.

sources.title: "The Junior League joins the world," Maclean's, November 24, 1956
sources.notes: States that as of 1956, 'for thirty-six years' (i.e. since ~1920) the Junior League 'has given nearly four hundred underprivileged girls a three-week vacation' at a Laurentians camp; Montreal branch was then the oldest in Canada, 511 members. Full article paywalled (archive.macleans.ca returned 400); accessed via search snippet only.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1994 (English)
sources.notes: States under 'Kamp Kanawana': 'This was Kanawana's 100th year of operation. As part of the centennial celebration, an Alumni reunion was held during Labor Day weekend attracting over 200 past campers and staff.' Also: 101% camper-registration capacity, 70% return rate, 40 subsidized campers (+10% over 1993).

sources.title: YMCA de Montreal, Rapport annuel, 1994 (French)
sources.notes: French-language sibling of src_ia_ymca_annual_1994, same centennial/reunion content.

sources.title: YMCA de Montreal, Rapport annuel, 1989 (French)
sources.notes: Describes the 'Centenary of YMCA Camping in Canada' (1889-1989, marking 100 years since Big Cove/Halifax YMCA 1889) -- a distinct, institution-wide event from Kanawana's own 1994 centennial. Kanawana and 28 other YMCA camps participated in a relay campfire (ashes from Big Cove distributed to every camp, each burning a campfire for 29 hours comparing songs/legends/customs, culminating in a time capsule buried at the CCA's October congress). Also documents a 5-year, $250,000 facility 'rajeunissement' (rejuvenation) campaign at Kamp Kanawana, and names the 1988-89 Kamp Kanawana Committee: Andre Herard, Chris Adam, Keith Farquharson, Paul Cappelli, Derek Walsh, Tom Snabl, Bruce Netherwood, Maureen McBride, Jay Netherwood, Bill Pigott.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1990
sources.notes: Lists 'Netherwood, Bruce (Director, Kamp Kanawana)' and separately 'Netherwood, Jay (Supervisor, Kamp Kanawana)' -- Jay remained on staff in a supervisory role after Bruce took the Director title. Also describes a 5-year strategic building-planning process covering the Downtown YMCA, Kamp Kanawana, and the Du Parc YMCA.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1971-72
sources.notes: States: 'A ski tow has been installed there to broaden the scope of winter programming' -- the earliest documented step toward Kanawana's Winter Outdoor Family Camping program.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report, 1972-73
sources.notes: Precisely dates the Winter Outdoor Family Camping program to winter 1972-73: 'A ski lift has already been installed there, two slopes have been groomed for downhill runs and miles of trails marked for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing... Courses of instruction were carried on for all ages, and a babysitting service enabled parents with toddlers to take part in activities.'

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal (Quebec) Annual Report, 1996
sources.notes: States: 'This was the first time that programs were offered to groups other than summer campers. A group of 50 Korean students... participated in traditional camp activities for four days, sleeping in tents, cooking on open fires and integrating with the campers.' This is an in-season (summer) international-group visit, distinct from -- and not direct confirmation of -- the separately-sourced claim that year-round RESIDENTIAL programming began in 1996; the two claims may be related but are not shown to be the same thing.

sources.title: Wikipedia / reporting on Leslie Paris (UBC) research — "Color war" (summer camp tradition)
sources.notes: The general team-competition-week genre (of which Kanawana's Lumbermen/Voyageur Games is a Canadian-YMCA-frontier-themed variant) is documented by historian Leslie Paris as originating with 'Red and Gray Week' in 1916 at Schroon Lake Camp, a Jewish boys' camp in the Adirondacks, becoming a widespread camp staple by the 1920s.

sources.title: YMCA Quebec — "Voyageurs" canoe-tripping program page
sources.notes: Confirms the modern Kanawana canoe-tripping program for ages 13-16 is itself branded 'Voyageurs' (separate from the L&V Games team of the same name), with a flat-water option in La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve alongside whitewater options (Coulonge, Dumoine, Noire rivers) -- appears to be parallel reuse of 'voyageur' branding across two distinct camp institutions, not the L&V Games tradition literally expanding into a canoe-trip program.

sources.title: American Camp Association — Hedley S. Dimock Award press releases, 2022-2026
sources.notes: Direct WebFetch of each year's ACA press release page confirmed recipients: 2022 Simone Gamble (NY & NJ), Tracey Gaslin PhD (Ohio); 2023 Matt Buczek (NY & NJ), Rachel Fendell Satinsky (Keystone); 2024 Elisa Spungen Bildner & Robert Bildner, Foundation for Jewish Camp (NY/NJ); 2025 Bashier Kayou (New England), Bethany Uhl MD (Ohio); 2026 John Hamilton (Heart of the South), Chris T. Rehs-Dupin (NY/NJ). 2015 recipients (Ellen S. Gannett, Lance Ozier) found only via search snippet (direct ACA page 403) -- medium confidence. 2019-2021 remain unresolved -- see priorities.json; two specific 2019 claims ('Florida Youth Conservation Centers Network' and 'David Bryfman') could not be adjudicated against a primary source and should NOT be added to the KB without independent verification.

sources.title: "YMCA: Kamp Kanawana (no sound)" — YouTube (Concordia University Records Management & Archives channel)
sources.notes: Uploaded by Concordia University Records Management & Archives, 2022-06-21. Description: 'P0145-09-0087: Various scenes from Kamp Kanawana from the 1960s, including swimming and diving.' Provides a citable URL for the 1960s silent Kanawana film already referenced in kanawana-in-media.md without a direct link.

sources.title: Commission de toponymie du Quebec -- additional "Lac Wilson" fiches (Brownsburg-Chatham, Saint-Theophile, Grenville-sur-la-Rouge)
sources.notes: Three official Quebec 'Lac Wilson' toponymy entries beyond the one already known (Sainte-Lucie-des-Laurentides, fiche 135620): Brownsburg-Chatham (fiche 451695) -- named for a landowning family, early 20th century, who also built a dam to create the lake; Saint-Theophile (fiche 67250) -- named for a man named Wilson who built a fishing camp; Grenville-sur-la-Rouge (fiche 67246) -- origin undetermined. 3 of 4 documented Quebec 'Lac Wilson' toponyms are named for a landowner/settler named Wilson.

sources.title: Concordia University AccessToMemory -- "Wilson Griffith McConnell collection" finding aid (search-snippet only)
sources.notes: Direct page fetch (and Wayback Machine mirror) both blocked -- a JS/cookie bot-challenge page ('Verifying Your Browser'). Content obtained only via a WebSearch snippet of the page: Wilson Griffith McConnell born March 3, 1908, managed St. Lawrence Sugar, was a jazz enthusiast/collector, died January 12, 1966. No mention of Camp Kanawana, YMCA, or Lake Wilson in the visible snippet -- low-medium confidence, not a full-text confirmation.

sources.title: Concordia University Archives finding aid -- YMCA of Montreal fonds sub-series 13E (Expo 1967/Canadian Centennial)
sources.notes: Lists an item, 'Expo 67-canoe tripping program. -- 1964' (Box HA1930). Does not name Kanawana explicitly -- a lead, not a confirmed Kanawana-Expo67 connection.

sources.title: Mes Aieux genealogy database -- Yves St-Pierre / Lucette Gregoire marriage record (1970)
sources.notes: Marriage record: Yves St-Pierre and Lucette Gregoire, married Napierville, Quebec, 1970. Matches the wife's name in the already-cited 2020 Montreal obituary of a Yves St-Pierre (age 76). Weak, corroborating-only evidence -- does not establish any YMCA/Kanawana/camp connection for this specific person.

sources.title: The Georgian (Sir George Williams University student newspaper) -- Internet Archive digitized collection
sources.notes: 200+ individual issues (vol. 1-33, covering 1936-37 and 1962-70) digitized by Concordia University Records Management and Archives. Merged with Loyola News in 1980 to form The Link. NOT yet searched for 'Kanawana' mentions -- archive.org's advancedsearch.php text: field does NOT perform true full-text OCR search (confirmed via a positive-control test using the 1969 SGW 'Computer Riot,' which the Georgian covered extensively but which also returned 0 results) -- only a human using the real browser-based search-inside feature, issue by issue, can properly search this collection.

sources.title: McGill Daily and Le Delit -- Internet Archive "McGill Student Publications Collection"
sources.notes: 9,868 issues, 1911-2001, fully digitized. Same search-API limitation as src_ia_the_georgian applies -- not yet properly searched for Kanawana mentions.

sources.title: French Wikipedia -- "Lac Landron"
sources.notes: Lac Landron is located in the unorganized territory of Lac-Lenotre, MRC La Vallee-de-la-Gatineau, Outaouais, inside the Zec Capitachouane -- east of, administratively adjacent to (not inside) La Verendrye Wildlife Reserve proper. Named for Pierre Landron; toponym officially registered December 5, 1968.

sources.title: French Wikipedia / SEPAQ -- Reserve faunique La Verendrye institutional history
sources.notes: Established 1939 as 'Reserve de la Route Mont-Laurier-Senneterre'; converted to a park and renamed in 1950 for the bicentennial of explorer La Verendrye's 1749 death; now a 'reserve faunique' under SEPAQ.

sources.title: Radio-Canada / La Presse -- SEPAQ takeover of canoe-camping administration in Reserve La Verendrye (2022)
sources.notes: From 1993, canoe-camping in Reserve La Verendrye was managed by FQCC (Federation quebecoise du canot-camping, later Canot Kayak Quebec) in partnership with SEPAQ; around 2022 SEPAQ took over full/sole management. Describes the reserve's general public canoe-camping administration, NOT the YMCA's specific 1962-63 Lac Landron lease -- no source confirms the private lease's individual fate; current official Kanawana Voyageurs program pages make no mention of Lac Landron or any private base camp.

sources.title: Mike Cohen, "Back to Camp for Terry 'Aislin' Mosher as Kanawana gets set to honour master cartoonist," The Suburban blog (2015-08-01)
sources.notes: Direct Mosher quotes on his Kanawana camper years (favourite camp, remembers the layout, hasn't been back since 1954, five grandchildren who have/do/will attend); parents named Jack and Norma Mosher; states the 2015 Pip Award ceremony was Saturday, August 8, 2015 -- corroborated by a second YMCA Quebec newsroom URL, and consistent with a day-of-week check (Aug 3, 2015 was a Monday; Aug 8 was a Saturday) -- the already-cited 'August 3' date in src_ymca_pip_mosher is very likely a transcription error.

sources.title: Peter Kerr, "Terry Mosher - aka Aislin," The Montrealer (2016-02-14)
sources.notes: Extensive early-life biography (schools, expulsion incident, hitchhiking years, Canada Council grant, first/second marriages) -- not Kanawana-specific. States Order of Canada received 'in 1992' from GG Adrienne Clarkson -- almost certainly an error, since Clarkson was not GG until 1999; the existing article's 2003 date (Canadian Encyclopedia) remains more reliable.

sources.title: Twynam, G.D. & Johnston, M. (2004). "Changes in host community reactions to a special sporting event." Current Issues in Tourism, 7(3), 242-261
sources.notes: A previously undocumented Twynam/Johnston collaboration: a longitudinal study of Thunder Bay resident reactions to the 1995 Nordic World Ski Championships. Confirmed via two independent secondary citations plus a working DOI; the publisher's own abstract page returned 403 Forbidden, so full abstract text is unconfirmed (citation-level confidence only).

sources.title: Concordia University Archives -- Drummond Street YMCA building history
sources.notes: YMCA of Montreal moved from Dominion Square to Drummond Street in 1912 (cost $540,206); a 12-storey annex was added 1930-31; Sir George Williams University students used the building's chapel/gym/pool until the 1970s; 'The YMCA occupied the building until it was demolished in 2002.'

sources.title: YMCA Quebec newsroom -- "The sale of the downtown Montreal YMCA building" (October 11, 2023)
sources.notes: Announces intent to sell the rebuilt downtown Drummond/Stanley YMCA building, citing reduced post-COVID membership revenue, aging-infrastructure costs, and only one-third of the building being used for programming. Tenants (a language school ~3,400 students, TeenZone ~650, homelessness/reentry services) to continue 'until 2025.'

sources.title: Concordia University Archives finding aid -- YMCA of Montreal fonds sub-series 13D (Memorials, tributes, testimonials, honours)
sources.notes: Box HA2330 holds 'research reports on D.A. Budge' as part of Joyce Oliver's 1939-40 'Book of Remembrance and History' project (~50 biographical subjects researched for a YMCA commemorative history). Contents not yet read -- a concrete additional archival lead for D.A. Budge's biographical open questions.

sources.title: YMCA of Greater Toronto blog: "Celebrating Tradition with the Pine Crest Games"
sources.notes: YMCA Camp Pine Crest's 'Lumbermen vs Voyageurs' color-war games, running since 1940 -- a naming/structure parallel to Kanawana's L&V Games worth checking as a possible shared-origin lead.

sources.title: Wikimapia: Kamp Kanawana entry
sources.notes: States camp is '455 acres' vs YMCA's own current '550 acres' claim -- unresolved discrepancy. Page content could not be directly fetched/dated by the research agent (blocked); only the search-snippet acreage figure and promotional phrasing were confirmed.

sources.title: Ville de Saint-Sauveur, Plan d'urbanisme (draft, March 2024)
sources.notes: Municipal planning document explicitly states Kanawana's large natural spaces present environmental value 'meritant d'être reconnue' within the city's planning -- names the camp specifically but does not confer a formal designation.

sources.title: Ville de Saint-Sauveur, Règlement de zonage 222-2008 (consolidated)
sources.notes: Defines an 'Affectation récréative et de conservation (RC)' zoning category whose stated example use is a 'camp de vacances'; a 'RC 123' zone code appears near a Sainte-Elmire road reference but the camp parcel's actual zone could not be confirmed from extracted text (zone maps are graphical).

sources.title: Montreal Gazette, "Summer Camps – Kanawana" (April 18, 1974)
sources.notes: Located but paywalled (HTTP 403 to automated fetch) -- a concrete, specific lead for the section-gender-reassignment dating question. Requires the operator's own Newspapers.com public-access account to read.

sources.title: History of Canadian Broadcasting: Robert (Rob) Braide
sources.notes: Full career biography including the claim that Braide chaired the YMCA's Kamp Kanawana Capital Campaign.

sources.title: Billboard Canada: "Rob Braide's Remarkable, Storied Career in Broadcasting"
sources.notes: Career retrospective corroborating broadcasting-history.ca's biography of Rob Braide.

sources.title: Gulf Islands Driftwood: obituary of David Ian William Braide (1928-2018)
sources.notes: Obituary of a separate Braide family patriarch (Montreal businessman, 36-year career at Canadian Industries Limited) whose obituary names YMCA board roles including 'the Montreal and Westmount YMCAs.' Names son Robbie David Braide, father of Ian and Vicki Braide (Kanawana campers/CITs 2000-2007). No confirmed link to Rob Braide the broadcaster (b. 1953).

sources.title: YMCA Camp Manitou-Lin (Grand Rapids, MI): camp history page
sources.notes: Comparative cross-camp data point: 'Uncle Bob' Augustine held the title Resident Director in 1931, then Camp Director from 1932-1948 at this unrelated YMCA camp -- suggests 'Resident Director' functioned as a subordinate/precursor rank to 'Camp Director' at at least one other YMCA camp. Circumstantial only, not a Kanawana-specific or YMCA-of-Montreal-specific source.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal fonds (Internet Archive): Camp Perrot annual reports and brochures, 1945-1969
sources.notes: 11 Camp Perrot annual reports/brochures digitized by Concordia RMA (uploader archives@concordia.ca, addeddate 2024-05-13), collection 'ymca-montreal-fonds'. Identifiers include 1945-the-new-ymca-camp-on-isle-perrot-brochure, 1947-camp-perrot-brochure, and annual reports 1948-1954/1958. Verified genuine via direct archive.org metadata API fetch (not fabricated) -- addeddate/uploader/collection all confirmed. Read in full for location, founding date (triangulated to 1944), age range, capacity, and programming detail.

sources.title: "A Fresh Look at Camp Perrot" -- internal memo by director Donald Cochrane (1959)
sources.notes: Verified genuine via archive.org metadata API. Cochrane's first-person rebuttal of a July 1958 Camp Committee decision to close Camp Perrot once a new site was found; cites closure rationale (limited programme/site, encroaching homes, young counsellors, poor swimming, bank erosion) and defends the camp, including a direct Perrot-vs-Kanawana comparison in his own words and A. Ross Seaman's tree-planting c.1950.

sources.title: "Camp Perrot Family Centre" -- planning document (1969)
sources.notes: Verified genuine via archive.org metadata API. sources.title: Camp Pascobac official history page (camppascobac.ca/history.htm)
sources.notes: Camp Pascobac is at Kars, New Brunswick, on Belleisle Bay, Kings County -- NOT Manitoba. Land bought May 1928 by the Y's Men of Saint John for $650. 'Pascobac' is stated to be an Indigenous name meaning 'side bay'.

sources.title: "Brief Autobiographical Sketch of Association Career", August 1919
sources.notes: FIRST-PERSON MEMOIR BY A FOUNDING PARTICIPANT, written 25 years after the fact. The author is not named in the OCR (the signature is illegible) but is identifiable from internal evidence: he joined the Montreal YMCA in 1883, graduated in 1892, took charge of membership and finances at the new Dominion Square building, and in June 1894 became the THIRD General Secretary of the Winnipeg YMCA, succeeding Herbert Gill (the first was C. M. Copeland); later YMCA Area Supervisor for Military District No. 10 (Saskatchewan) 1916-1918. Key passage: "a small group composed of W. H. Ball, John W. Ross, Will Wilson, myself and others formed a small syndicate to investigate the possibilities of securing an opening for a young men's camp. St. Agathe District was visited by four of us... it was decided to locate the first camp at Lac la Croix and in 1894 the first group went out. It was then discovered that just a little further on there was a better location, and property with fishing privileges was secured at Lac St. Joseph." This CONFLICTS with the established narrative that the 1894 camp was at Lake Saint-Joseph -- see conflict c_024. Also independently names "John W. Ross", bearing on the John Roy / John W. Ross identification question.

sources.title: The Lookout, Vol. 1 No. 3 — Kanawana Alumni newsletter, autumn 1993
sources.notes: Only issue of this alumni newsletter in the digitized corpus; the numbering implies at least two earlier issues and any 1994 centennial issues would be richer still. Carries: Richard "Itche" Kerr's FIRST-PERSON account of writing the camp song at the end of summer 1977; a list of past directors the alumni association was seeking addresses for ("David Twynam (79-82), Tom Potts (part of 72), Jim Turner (?-71), Jeff Anderson (?)") -- the only source for Tom Potts in 1972; the 1993 L&V result (Voyageurs, narrowly), twice, once as an eyewitness account of the closing banquet; Bruce Netherwood signing as Director; a memorial for song-leader Maureen McBride (d. 8 May 1993); and the phrase "the ancient plaques that haunt the dining hall".

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Annual Report 1894-1895 (fiscal year ending 30 April 1895)
sources.notes: THE FOUNDING DOCUMENT. Junior Department report: "We are able to report the holding of our first Summer Camp, which was in every way a decided success... This Camp was composed of 23 workers and boys." Statistical summary confirms "Attendance at Summer Camp ... 23". The Physical Department section of the SAME report separately records the leased land and fishing rights near Ste-Agathe used by 53 adult members -- two parallel streams, Junior and Senior, on one lake. Officers list carries the first Summer Camp committee: "John W. Ross, Chairman. E. J. Coyle. R. L. Charlton." CRITICAL NULL: the word "Jubilee" appears in this report ONLY in the YMCA-worldwide golden-jubilee sense (1844-1894), never as a camp name.

sources.title: YMCA of Montreal Fifty-Ninth Annual Report, for the year ending 30 April 1910
sources.notes: ANNOUNCES KANAWANA IN THE FORWARD TENSE, fixing its first season as summer 1910: "A new site has been secured for the Boys Camp on Lake Kanawana, near Shawbridge... a summer vacation camp for boys, from July 1st to August 15th. They will have accommodation for 70 boys. This camp will be under the charge of Mr. W. J. Holliday, of the Central Branch. The Summer Camp at Lac St. Joseph will have renewed equipment, and will be given over entirely to the senior members." The masthead already lists them separately: "Men's Summer Camp, - Lac St. Joseph / Boys' Summer Camp, - Lake Kanawana."

sources.notes: THE AUTHORITATIVE FINDING AID, and a strict superset of the static-HTML mirror this project had been working from. 173 sub-series and sub-sub-series units against the mirror's 95; every mirror page corresponds to a unit here, and 78 units have no mirror page at all. Reached via the /downloads/ path, which is NOT behind the AtoM browser challenge that blocks concordia.accesstomemory.org itself. PDF and extracted text both cached. NOTE ON THE CACHE: the repo's .gitignore excludes *.pdf, so only the extracted .txt is committed. The PDF is re-fetchable at the origin_url with a plain curl -- no challenge, no auth.

sources.title: Concordia University Archives — AtoM catalogue (concordia.accesstomemory.org)
sources.notes: ACCESS STATUS, 2026-08-25. The live AtoM catalogue at concordia.accesstomemory.org serves every request -- including its own OAI-PMH endpoint, which exists only for machines -- behind a JavaScript challenge. The challenge sets atom_js and atom_headless, the latter carrying base64('<value>:'+navigator.webdriver). Sequence of attempts: (1) Playwright/Chromium -- failed for an UNRELATED reason, Chromium cannot reach this environment's egress proxy (example.com failed identically), so this is our constraint, not Concordia's; (2) honest declaration, webdriver=true, cookies verified on the wire -- REFUSED; (3) on explicit operator authorization (M. Aronson, 2026-08-25, on the basis that the control targets malicious scraping and that Concordia's robots.txt is 'User-agent: * / Crawl-delay: 60'), webdriver=false -- ALSO REFUSED. The server checks something beyond that flag. Further reverse-engineering of the challenge was STOPPED: the operator's authorization cannot be traced to Concordia, who are the only party able to grant it, and continuing would mean defeating a control the site owner deliberately placed on the catalogue. SANCTIONED ROUTES THAT WORK: (a) the 125-page PDF finding aid at /downloads/ymca-of-montreal-fonds-2.pdf -- NOT behind the challenge, already cached here, and the authoritative description of all 173 units; (b) an operator-side fetch from a normal browser; (c) archives@concordia.ca. Note that archives.concordia.ca is NOT this catalogue -- it redirects to the university CMS.

sources.title: Account of the 2026 Montreal bus-point move from Pierre-Laporte to Westmount High School (operator-supplied)
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) account, supplied 2026-08-28, giving the specific chain of events behind the change the 2026 parent guide attributes only to 'circumstances beyond our control' (f_2314). The operator is a participant in the account he is supplying -- he is one of the actors in it -- which is noted wherever it is cited. Uncorroborated by any document held here; it does not conflict with any documented source, it fills a gap the documents deliberately leave blank. The named third party, Chris Manitt, is recorded by institutional role only (former Kanawana staff member; chairman of the governing board at Westmount High School) per the standing Phase 2 privacy rule; the Westmount High School principal, whom the operator did not name, is left unnamed.

sources.title: Recall of the 1995 Counsellor-in-Training cohort (operator-supplied)
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) recall, 2026-08-28, naming six of the 1995 CITs and stating explicitly that there were more he could not recall -- so this is a PARTIAL list offered as partial, not a roster. Supplied to place Chris Manitt at camp (p_289). Three of the six (Dan Aronson, Marina Sharpe, Avigail Aronoff) are independently corroborated by the documented 'CITS 95' plaque (f_1614); one (Chris Manitt) and one (Tiffany Ballhorn) are absent from it; one (Erin MacIntyre) shares a first name with the plaque's Erin McKenzie and may or may not be the same person -- see conflict c_027. The operator was himself a Junior Counsellor in 1994 and a Packer in 1995-96, so he was on site the season he is recalling.

sources.title: Operator correction: the 1995 CIT was Erin McKenzie, not Erin MacIntyre
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) withdrew his own recalled surname on being shown the 'CITS 95' plaque transcription: 'It was Erin McKenzie, I misremembered the surname.' Resolves c_027 to one person, not two, in the documented source's favour. Note the direction of the correction -- the operator corrected himself against the document rather than the reverse; the 2026-07-07 directive was never invoked.

sources.title: Operator identification of the illegible 1993 CIT plaque name: Alex Ballhorn
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) supplied the fourth faint name at the foot of column 1 on the 'C.I.T.'s of '93' plaque: Alex Ballhorn. The operator is himself named on that plaque as a 1993 CIT, so this is recall of his own cohort. It OVERTURNS an inference recorded hours earlier in f_1568, which had used the plaque's alphabetical ordering to argue the slot could not take 'Ballhorn'. On being told the name, the faint glyphs read as 'Alex Ballhorn' without strain. No conflict record: the plaque is ILLEGIBLE at that point, not contradictory -- oral history filling an unreadable span is exactly the case the 2026-07-07 directive leaves to oral history.

sources.title: Operator confirmation: Alex and Tiff Bollhorn were siblings; the surname is spelled Bollhorn
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) confirms the sibling relationship between the 1993 and 1995 CITs and settles the FAMILY spelling as BOLLHORN. He then corrected this agent's handling of it -- 'No, it was my memory, you were right' -- identifying the wrong spelling as originating in his own recall ('Tiffany Ballhorn'), not in the agent's reading of the 1993 plaque. Verified against the session transcript and upheld: the agent read 'Alex Ballhorn' off the plaque at 2026-08-28T14:35:26Z, BEFORE the operator named Alex at all (2026-08-30T02:08:02Z). The reading was independent. See f_2329, which now records a real divergence between the family spelling and the 1993 plaque's paint.

sources.title: Operator account of the Rangers / Wolf / Trailblazers / Foresters programme lineage
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) supplied the lineage of Kanawana's leadership programmes, unprompted, on being shown the plaque audit's 'Wolf' finding. It CORRECTS an inference of mine -- I had read the 2009 boards' 'WOLF' credit as a third staff title; it is a PROGRAMME name. It also dates two programmes the wiki records as 'entirely undated' (Trailblazers, Foresters) and closes a 34-year gap in the Rangers record.

sources.title: Operator refinement: WOLF beside a name was a rank, like CIT or LIT
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson): 'I think that WOLF when written next to a name was a rank/role - like a CIT or LIT.' RELIABILITY SET TO SECONDARY, not primary, because the operator hedges it ('I think') -- unlike his flat statements about the programme lineage in src_oral_aronson_rangers_wolf_lineage, which are recorded as primary. This refines rather than overturns f_2345: it does not restore the discarded 'third staff role' reading, and the junior-to-staff progression count stays at 44.

sources.title: Operator answers to p_300: the Sanctum, the Suez Bridge, and Raku
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) answering the three questions queued as p_300, all of which the plaque audit had raised and no document held here could settle. Stated flatly, without hedging. NOTE ON SPELLING: the operator writes 'Joanna Hode', which is the exact misspelling this wiki carried before correcting it to Joanna A.A. Hoad against Lower Canada College's archived staff records (f_1730, f_1755) -- almost certainly the origin of the original error, since that entry also came from his oral history. The corrected spelling is used throughout; the recurrence is noted because it shows the error was in the source, not in the transcription.

sources.title: Operator: Julien and Yves Tasse are father and son
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson) first said brothers, then corrected himself unprompted within the same exchange to FATHER AND SON. The correction is the operative statement and is what is recorded; the initial answer is noted here only because a self-correction made that quickly is a signal about the care of the source, not a conflict to resolve. He did NOT say which is the father -- that is inferred below from the plaque chronology and is flagged as an inference wherever it appears.

sources.title: Operator: Julien Tasse, camp caretaker 30+ years; the dining hall renamed Salle Julien Tasse
sources.notes: Operator (Matt Aronson): Julien Tasse was the camp's caretaker for 30+ years, died c.1992-95, and the DINING HALL was technically renamed SALLE JULIEN TASSE after his death, though the name never stuck in use. This OVERTURNS an inference recorded minutes earlier in f_2356 -- that Julien was a boy on the 1963-64 Advance Guard boards -- and it removes him from the junior-to-staff progression count, since he was staff throughout. Note the operator was a camper and staff member 1985-2002, i.e. present at the camp during the renaming and well placed on it; his death date is given as a range, which is preserved rather than narrowed.

sources.title: YMCA of Greater Halifax/Dartmouth, 165 Years of Community Building (anniversary yearbook)
sources.read_state_basis: direct: 52-page PDF fetched and text-extracted locally with pypdf 2026-09-05; all five Big Cove pages read
sources.notes: The camp owner's own anniversary publication. Contains BOTH the claim that Big Cove is 'the oldest continuously running residential camp in Canada' (p.8) AND a timeline entry recording that resident camping ceased after 1975 and resumed only in 1980 (p.28). WebFetch's markdown converter returned binary garbage; the PDF was extracted locally instead -- a fact about the tool, not the document.

sources.title: Camp Stephens Alumni blog (YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg)
sources.notes: Same alumni blog already cited in c_029 for the Nelson McEwen CCA-founding claim. Carries the December 2020 statement that COVID restrictions made 2020 'the first closure since 1917', and the claim that Camp Stephens is 'the longest-serving summer camp in Canada'.

sources.title: YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg -- Camp Stephens pages (About Us, History)
sources.notes: Camp Stephens' own current site. Gives 1891 Keewatin Beach, 1893 islands located, 1896 name adopted, 'over 130 years'. EXPLICIT NULL: says nothing about any closure, including 1917/1918 or COVID.

sources.title: Big Cove YMCA Camp -- YMCA of Greater Halifax and Dartmouth (camp page)
sources.notes: Claims 'Canada's oldest overnight camp' with roots 'back to 1889'. EXPLICIT NULL: no mention of the 1976-79 gap.

sources.title: CBC News, "In the summers without summer camps, staff get creative to stay afloat" (Big Cove and Kadimah)
sources.read_state_basis: cbc.ca returns HTTP 403 to the fetch tool while serving browsers -- the same refuse-the-tool pattern this project documented in Part 12. Content known only through search-engine result summaries, NOT read directly.
sources.notes: Reports that Big Cove ran no overnight camp in 2020 but rented cabins to families, operated as a campground with canoeing and archery in 2021 while sustaining itself through its leadership training programme, and returned to normal operations in 2022. NOT DIRECTLY READ -- see read_state.
